‘There are three things too wonderful for me to understand—yes, four that I do not know:
‘The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a snake on a rock; the way of a ship in the middle of the sea; and the way of a man with a young woman.’
I

The utter desolation of the landscape was beginning to affect me. I sat down to face my situation and, if possible, remember some landmark that might help me find my way out. If only I could find the ocean again, everything would be clear, for I knew the island of Groix was visible from the cliffs.
I put down my gun, knelt behind a rock, and lit a pipe. Then I looked at my watch. It was nearly four o’clock. Since daybreak I might have wandered a long way from Kerselec.

The day before, I had stood with Goulven on the cliffs below Kerselec, looking out over the sombre moors where I was now lost. Those uplands had seemed as flat as a meadow, stretching to the horizon. Although I knew how deceptive distance can be, I had not realised that what looked from Kerselec like mere grassy hollows were great valleys covered in gorse and heather. What had seemed scattered boulders were actually enormous granite cliffs.

‘It’s a bad place for a stranger,’ old Goulven had said. ‘You’d better take a guide.’ I had replied, ‘I won’t get lost.’ Now, as I sat smoking with the sea wind in my face, I knew that I was lost. On every side the moorland stretched away, covered in flowering gorse, heather and granite boulders. There was not a tree in sight, let alone a house. After a while I picked up the gun, turned my back to the sun, and trudged on again.

There was little point in following any of the noisy streams that crossed my path from time to time. Instead of flowing to the sea, they ran inland to reedy pools in the moors’ hollows. I had followed several, but each led to a swamp or a silent little pond. Snipe rose from them with piping cries and wheeled away in a frenzy of fear. I was growing tired, and the gun chafed my shoulder despite its double padding. The sun sank lower and lower, shining horizontally across the yellow gorse and the moorland pools.

As I walked, my own gigantic shadow led me on, seeming to lengthen with every step. Gorse scraped my leggings and crackled beneath my feet, showering the brown earth with flowers. The ferns bent and billowed along my path. Rabbits darted from clumps of heather through the bracken, and I heard the sleepy quack of wild ducks among the marsh grass. Once a fox slipped across my path. Another time, as I bent to drink from a rushing little stream, a heron flapped heavily out of the reeds beside me. I turned to look at the sun. It seemed to touch the edge of the plain. Finally I decided there was no point in continuing, and that I must accept spending at least one night on the moors. Completely worn out, I threw myself down. The evening sunlight slanted warmly across my body, but the sea winds were rising, and a chill struck through me from my wet shooting boots. High overhead, gulls wheeled and tossed like scraps of white paper. A lone curlew called from a distant marsh. Little by little, the sun sank into the plain, and the sky overhead flushed with its afterglow. I watched it change from palest gold to pink, then to smouldering fire. Clouds of midges danced above me, and high in the still air a bat dipped and soared. My eyelids began to droop. Then, as I shook off my drowsiness, a sudden crash in the bracken startled me. I looked up. A great bird hovered, quivering in the air above my face. For an instant I stared, unable to move. Then something leapt past me through the ferns, and the bird rose, wheeled and plunged headlong into the bracken.

In an instant I was on my feet, peering through the gorse. I heard a struggle in a clump of heather nearby, then silence. I stepped forward with my gun ready. But when I reached the heather, I lowered it under my arm again and stood motionless in silent astonishment. A dead hare lay on the ground, and a magnificent falcon stood on it, one talon buried in the creature’s neck, the other firmly planted on its limp flank. What astonished me was not simply the sight of a falcon on its prey. I had seen that more than once. The falcon had a sort of leash fitted round both talons, with a round piece of metal like a sleigh bell hanging from it. The bird turned its fierce yellow eyes on me, then bent and drove its curved beak into its prey. At that instant hurried footsteps sounded in the heather, and a girl sprang into the thicket ahead. Without glancing at me, she went up to the falcon, slipped her gloved hand beneath its breast, and lifted it from the hare. Then she deftly pulled a small hood over its head. Holding it out on her gauntlet, she bent and picked up the hare.

She tied a cord round the animal’s legs and fastened its end to her belt. Then she started back through the thicket. As she passed, I lifted my cap, and she acknowledged me with an almost imperceptible nod. I had been so astonished, so absorbed in admiration of the scene, that it had not occurred to me that she could save me. But as she moved away, I remembered that unless I wanted to sleep on a windswept moor that night, I had better find my voice at once. At my first word she hesitated. As I stepped in front of her, I thought a look of fear came into her beautiful eyes. But when I humbly explained my unpleasant predicament, she blushed and looked at me in wonder.
‘Surely you didn’t come from Kerselec!’ she repeated.

Her sweet voice had no trace of a Breton accent, or any other accent I knew. Yet there was something in it that I seemed to have heard before: something quaint and impossible to define, like the melody of an old song.
I explained that I was an American, unfamiliar with Finistère, and was shooting there for my own amusement.
‘An American,’ she repeated in those same quaint, musical tones. ‘I have never seen an American before.’
She stood silent for a moment, then looked at me and said, ‘Even if you walked all night, you couldn’t reach Kerselec now, not even with a guide.’
This was pleasant news.
‘But,’ I began, ‘if only I could find a peasant’s cottage where I could get something to eat and some shelter.’
The falcon on her wrist fluttered and shook its head. She stroked its glossy back and glanced at me.
‘Look around,’ she said gently. ‘Can you see where these moors end? Look north, south, east and west. Can you see anything except moorland and bracken?’
‘No,’ I said.
‘The moor is wild and desolate. It’s easy to enter, but sometimes those who enter never leave. There are no peasants’ cottages here.’
‘Well,’ I said, ‘if you tell me which direction Kerselec is in, it won’t take me any longer to get back tomorrow than it took me to come.’
She looked at me again, with something almost like pity.
‘Ah,’ she said, ‘coming is easy and takes hours. Going is different—and may take centuries.’
I stared at her in astonishment, but decided I must have misunderstood. Before I could speak, she took a whistle from her belt and blew it.
‘Sit down and rest,’ she told me. ‘You’ve come a long way, and you’re tired.’
She gathered up her pleated skirts and beckoned me to follow. Picking her way delicately through the gorse, she led me to a flat rock among the ferns.

‘They’ll be here soon,’ she said. She sat at one end of the rock and invited me to sit on the other edge. The afterglow was fading from the sky, and a single star twinkled faintly through the rosy haze. A long, wavering triangle of waterbirds drifted southwards overhead. Plovers called from the surrounding marshes.
‘These moors are very beautiful,’ she said quietly.
‘Beautiful, but cruel to strangers,’ I answered.
‘Beautiful and cruel,’ she repeated dreamily. ‘Beautiful and cruel.’
‘Like a woman,’ I said stupidly.
‘Oh!’ she cried, catching her breath a little as she looked at me. Her dark eyes met mine, and I thought she seemed angry or frightened.
‘Like a woman,’ she repeated under her breath. ‘How cruel to say that!’ Then, after a pause, as though speaking aloud to herself, ‘How cruel of him to say that!’

I do not know what sort of apology I offered for that foolish, though harmless, remark. But she seemed so troubled by it that I began to think I had unknowingly said something dreadful. With horror, I remembered the traps and pitfalls the French language sets for foreigners. While I was trying to imagine what I might have said, voices sounded across the moor, and she stood up.
‘No,’ she said, with a trace of a smile on her pale face. ‘I won’t accept your apologies, sir. But I must prove you wrong, and that will be my revenge. Look. Here come Hastur and Raoul.’

Two men appeared out of the twilight. One carried a sack over his shoulders. The other carried a hoop in front of him as a waiter carries a tray. Straps fastened it to his shoulders, and three hooded falcons with tinkling bells sat round its edge. The girl approached the falconer and, with a quick turn of her wrist, transferred her falcon to the hoop. It immediately shuffled sideways and nestled among its companions, who shook their hooded heads and ruffled their feathers until the bells on their leg-straps tinkled again. The other man came forward, bowed respectfully, took the hare and dropped it into his game bag.
‘These are my huntsmen,’ she said, turning to me with gentle dignity. ‘Raoul is a good falconer, and one day I shall make him master of the hunt. Hastur has no equal.’
The two silent men greeted me respectfully.
‘Didn’t I tell you, sir, that I would prove you wrong?’ she continued. ‘This is my revenge: you must do me the courtesy of accepting food and shelter at my house.’

Before I could answer, she spoke to the falconers. They immediately set off across the heath. With a gracious gesture inviting me to accompany her, she followed. I do not know whether I made her understand how deeply grateful I was, but she seemed pleased to listen as we walked through the dew-covered heather.
‘Aren’t you very tired?’ she asked.
In her presence I had completely forgotten my exhaustion, and I told her so.

‘Don’t you think your gallantry is a little old-fashioned?’ she said. When I looked confused and humbled, she added quietly, ‘Oh, I like it. I like everything old-fashioned, and it’s delightful to hear you say such pretty things.’

The moorland around us was very still now beneath its ghostly sheet of mist. The plovers had stopped calling. The crickets and all the little creatures of the fields fell silent as we passed, though I thought I could hear them beginning again far behind us. Well ahead, the two tall falconers strode through the heather. The faint jingling of the hawks’ bells reached us in distant, murmuring chimes.

Suddenly a splendid hound dashed out of the mist ahead, followed by another and another, until half a dozen or more were bounding and leaping around the girl beside me. She stroked and quietened them with her gloved hand, speaking in quaint terms I remembered seeing in old French manuscripts.

Then the falcons on the hoop carried by the man ahead began to beat their wings and scream. From somewhere out of sight, the notes of a hunting horn floated across the moor. The hounds sprang ahead and vanished into the twilight. The falcons flapped and shrieked on their perch, and the girl picked up the horn’s tune and began to hum. Her voice sounded clear and mellow in the night air.
‘Hunter, hunter, hunt again; Leave Rosette and Jeanneton. Tonton, tonton, tontaine, tonton. Or, to drive the game at dawn, Let the Cupids stand on duty. Tonton, tontaine, tonton.’

As I listened to her lovely voice, a grey mass appeared ahead and rapidly became more distinct. The horn rang out joyfully above the clamour of hounds and falcons. A torch glimmered at a gate, and light streamed through an opening door. We stepped onto a wooden bridge that trembled beneath our feet, then rose behind us, creaking and straining, as we crossed the moat into a small stone courtyard enclosed by walls. A man came from an open doorway, bowed in greeting, and offered a cup to the girl beside me. She took it, touched it to her lips, then lowered it and turned to me. ‘I welcome you,’ she said softly.

At that moment one of the falconers brought another cup. Before handing it to me, he presented it to the girl, who tasted it. He made a gesture to take it back, but she hesitated. Then she stepped forward and offered me the cup with her own hands. I felt this was an extraordinarily gracious act, but hardly knew what was expected of me, and did not immediately lift it to my lips. She blushed crimson. I saw that I must act quickly.
‘Miss,’ I faltered, ‘a stranger whom you have saved from dangers he may never understand drinks this cup to the kindest and loveliest hostess in France.’

‘In His name,’ she murmured, crossing herself as I emptied the cup. Then she stepped into the doorway, turned to me with a charming gesture, and took my hand. Leading me into the house, she said again and again, ‘You are very welcome. You are truly welcome to the Château d’Ys.’
II

I woke the next morning with the music of the horn in my ears. Leaping out of the ancient bed, I went to a curtained window where sunlight filtered through small, deeply set panes. The horn stopped as I looked down into the courtyard.

A man who might have been the brother of the previous night’s two falconers stood among a pack of hounds. A curved horn was strapped across his back, and he held a whip with a long lash. The dogs whined and yelped, dancing around him in anticipation. Horses were stamping in the walled yard too.

‘Mount!’ cried a voice in Breton. With a clatter of hooves, the two falconers rode into the courtyard among the hounds, falcons on their wrists. Then I heard another voice that sent the blood throbbing through my heart. ‘Piriou Louis, hunt the hounds well, and spare neither spur nor whip. You, Raoul, and you, Gaston, see that the sparrowhawk doesn’t behave like a nestling. And if you think it best, give the bird its reward. Putting a bird out in the fresh air, like the moulted captive hawk on Hastur’s wrist, isn’t difficult. But you, Raoul, may not find it so easy to manage that adult, wild-caught hawk. Twice last week he foamed at live prey and lost his morsel, although he’s used to the lure. The bird behaves like a stupid young brancher. Feeding an adult, wild-caught hawk isn’t so easy.’

Was I dreaming? The old language of falconry I had read in yellowed manuscripts—the old, forgotten French of the Middle Ages—was sounding in my ears. The hounds bayed and the hawks’ bells tinkled in accompaniment to the stamping horses. She spoke again in that sweet, forgotten language:

‘If you’d rather attach the leash and leave your adult, wild-caught hawk on its block perch, Raoul, I won’t object. It would be a pity to spoil such a fine day’s sport with a badly trained, unmoulted youngster. Slim him down, reduce his food—perhaps that’s the best way. It will give him strength. Perhaps I was hasty with the bird. It takes time to work through the training line and the exercises with live quarry.’
Then the falconer Raoul bowed in his stirrups and replied, ‘If that is the young lady’s wish, I shall keep the hawk.’
‘It is my wish,’ she answered. ‘I know falconry, but you still have many lessons to give me in hunting with goshawks, my poor Raoul. Mr. Piriou Louis, mount!’
The huntsman sprang into an archway. A moment later he returned on a strong black horse, followed by another mounted huntsman.
‘Ah!’ she cried joyfully. ‘Hurry, Glemarec René! Hurry! Hurry, all of you! Sound your horn, Mr. Piriou!’

The silvery music of the hunting horn filled the courtyard. The hounds leapt through the gateway, and galloping hoofbeats rushed out of the paved court. They rang loudly on the drawbridge, suddenly became muffled, then disappeared into the moors’ heather and bracken. The horn sounded further and further away, until it was so faint that the sudden song of a rising lark drowned it in my ears. Below, I heard her voice answering a call from inside the house.
‘I don’t regret missing the hunt. I’ll go another time. Courtesy to the stranger, Pelagie, remember!’
A feeble voice trembled from inside the house: ‘Courtesy.’

I stripped and rubbed myself down from head to foot with the icy water in the huge earthenware basin standing on the stone floor at the foot of my bed. Then I looked for my clothes. They were gone. On a high-backed bench near the door lay a pile of garments, which I examined in astonishment. Since my clothes had vanished, I had to put on the outfit evidently left there for me to wear while my own things dried. Everything was there: cap, shoes and a hunting jacket of silvery-grey homespun cloth. But the close-fitting outfit and seamless shoes belonged to another century. I remembered the strange clothes worn by the three falconers in the courtyard. I was certain this was not the modern dress of any part of France or Brittany. But only when I was dressed and stood before a mirror between the windows did I realise I looked far more like a young medieval huntsman than a present-day Breton. I hesitated and picked up the cap. Should I go downstairs and show myself in this strange outfit? There seemed no alternative. My own clothes were gone, and there was no bell in the ancient room to summon a servant. I therefore did no more than remove a short hawk’s feather from the cap, open the door and go downstairs.

An old Breton woman sat spinning with a spinning staff beside the fireplace in the large room at the bottom of the stairs. When I appeared, she looked up, smiled openly, and wished me good health in Breton. I replied in French, laughing. At that moment my hostess appeared and returned my greeting with a grace and dignity that sent a thrill through my heart. Her lovely head, with its dark curls, wore a headdress that settled any doubts about the period of my own clothes. Her slender figure was beautifully set off by a homespun hunting dress edged in silver, and one of her cherished hawks perched on her gauntleted wrist. With perfect simplicity she took my hand and led me into the courtyard garden. She sat down at a table and very sweetly invited me to sit beside her. Then, in her soft, quaint accent, she asked how I had spent the night, and whether wearing the clothes old Pelagie had left for me while I slept was much of an inconvenience. I looked at my own clothes and shoes drying in the sun by the garden wall, and hated them. How hideous they were beside the graceful outfit I now wore! Laughing, I told her so, but she agreed with complete seriousness.

‘We’ll throw them away,’ she said quietly. Astonished, I tried to explain that I could not think of accepting clothes from anyone, although for all I knew this might be part of hospitality in that region. Besides, I would look quite absurd if I returned to France dressed as I was.

She laughed and tossed her pretty head, saying something in old French that I did not understand. Then Pelagie trotted out with a tray holding two bowls of milk, a loaf of white bread, fruit, a plate of honeycomb and a large jug of deep red wine. ‘You see, I haven’t had breakfast yet because I wanted you to eat with me. But I’m very hungry,’ she said, smiling.
‘I would rather die than forget a single word you’ve said!’ I blurted out, my cheeks burning. ‘She’ll think I’m mad,’ I told myself. But she turned to me with sparkling eyes.
‘Ah!’ she murmured. ‘Then you, sir, know everything there is to know about chivalry—’
She crossed herself and broke the bread. I sat watching her white hands, not daring to lift my eyes to hers.
‘Won’t you eat?’ she asked. ‘Why do you look so troubled?’

Ah, why? Now I knew. I knew I would give my life to touch those rosy palms with my lips. I understood that I had loved her from the moment I looked into her dark eyes on the moor the night before. My great, sudden passion left me speechless.
‘Are you uneasy?’ she asked again.

Then, like a man pronouncing his own doom, I answered quietly, ‘Yes, I am uneasy because I love you.’ She neither moved nor answered. The same power moved my lips against my will, and I said, ‘I, who am unworthy of your slightest thought; I, who abuse your hospitality and repay your gentle courtesy with bold presumption—I love you.’
She rested her head on her hands and answered softly, ‘I love you. Your words are very dear to me. I love you.’
‘Then I shall win you.’
‘Win me,’ she replied.

But all that time I had been sitting silently, my face turned towards her. She too sat silent, facing me, her sweet face resting on her upturned palm. As her eyes met mine, I knew that neither of us had spoken in human words. But I knew her soul had answered mine. I straightened, feeling youth and joyful love flowing through every vein. With a bright blush on her lovely face, she seemed to have woken from a dream. Her eyes sought mine with a questioning glance that made me tremble with delight. We ate breakfast, talking about ourselves. I told her my name, and she told me hers: Lady Jeanne d’Ys.

She told me of her father’s and mother’s deaths, and how she had spent her nineteen years in the little fortified farm, alone with her nurse Pelagie, the huntsman Glemarec René, and the four falconers—Raoul, Gaston, Hastur and Mr. Piriou Louis—who had served her father. She had never been outside the moorland. She had never even seen another human being except the falconers and Pelagie. She did not know how she had heard of Kerselec; perhaps the falconers had mentioned it. She knew the legends of Loup Garou and Jeanne la Flamme from her nurse Pelagie. She embroidered and spun flax. Her hawks and hounds were her only amusements. When she met me on the moor, the sound of my voice had frightened her so much that she had almost collapsed. It was true that she had seen ships at sea from the cliffs. But as far as she could see, the moors she galloped over showed no sign of human life. Old Pelagie told a legend that anyone lost in the unexplored moorland might never return, because the moors were enchanted. She did not know whether it was true. She had never thought about it until she met me. She did not know whether the falconers had ever been outside, or whether they could leave if they wanted to. The books in the house, which her nurse Pelagie had taught her to read, were hundreds of years old.

She told me all this with a sweet seriousness seldom found in anyone except children. She found my name easy to pronounce, and insisted that because my first name was Philip I must have French blood. She did not seem curious to learn anything about the outside world. I thought perhaps her nurse’s stories had made her feel it no longer deserved her interest or respect.
We were still sitting at the table. She was tossing grapes to the small field birds that came fearlessly right up to our feet.

I began to speak vaguely about leaving, but she would not hear of it. Before I knew it, I had promised to stay a week and hunt with hawk and hound in their company. I also gained permission to come back from Kerselec and visit her again after returning there.

‘Why,’ she said innocently, ‘I don’t know what I would do if you never came back.’ Knowing I had no right to awaken her with the sudden shock that declaring my own love would bring, I sat silent, scarcely daring to breathe.
‘Will you come very often?’ she asked.
‘Very often,’ I said.
‘Every day?’
‘Every day.’
‘Oh,’ she sighed, ‘I’m very happy. Come and see my hawks.’

She rose and took my hand again with a child’s innocent sense of possession. We walked through the garden and fruit trees to a grassy lawn bordered by a brook. Fifteen or twenty tree stumps, partly embedded in the grass, stood scattered over it. Falcons sat on all but two of them. They were tethered to the stumps with leather straps, which were in turn fastened by steel rivets to their legs just above the talons. A little stream of pure spring water wound its way within easy reach of every perch.
The birds raised a clamour when she appeared. She went from one to another, stroking some, lifting others briefly onto her wrist, or bending to adjust their leg straps.

‘Aren’t they beautiful?’ she said. ‘Look, here is a falcon-gentle. We call it “ignoble” because it catches its prey by chasing it directly. This is a blue falcon. In falconry we call it “noble” because it rises above its prey, circles, then drops on it from above. This white bird is a gyrfalcon from the north. It is “noble” too! Here is a merlin, and this male is a heron-hunting falcon.’
I asked how she had learned the old language of falconry. She could not remember, but thought her father must have taught her when she was very young.

Then she led me away and showed me the young falcons still in the nest. ‘In falconry, they’re called nestlings,’ she explained. ‘A brancher is a young bird just able to leave the nest and hop from branch to branch. A young bird that hasn’t yet moulted is called an unmoulted youngster, and a moulted captive is a hawk that has moulted in captivity. When we catch a wild falcon that has changed its plumage, we call it an adult, wild-caught falcon. Raoul first taught me to train a falcon. Shall I teach you how it’s done?’
She sat on the stream bank among the falcons, and I threw myself at her feet to listen.
Then Lady d’Ys held up one pink-tipped finger and began very seriously.
“First, one must catch the falcon.”
“I am caught,” I answered.
She laughed very prettily and told me that training me might be difficult, since I was noble.
“I am already tame,” I replied. “Fitted with leg straps and bells.”
She laughed in delight. “Oh, my brave falcon! Then you will return when I call?”
“I am yours,” I answered gravely.
She sat silently for a moment. Then the colour deepened in her cheeks. Raising her finger again, she said, “Listen. I want to speak of falconry—”
“I am listening, Countess Jeanne d’Ys.”
But she fell into a daydream again, her eyes seeming fixed on something beyond the summer clouds.
“Philip,” she said at last.
“Jeanne,” I whispered.
“That is all—that is what I wanted,” she sighed. “Philip and Jeanne.”
She held out her hand, and I touched it with my lips.
“Win me,” she said. But this time her body and soul spoke together.
After a while, she began again. “Let us speak of falconry.”
“Begin,” I replied. “We have caught the falcon.”

Then Jeanne d’Ys took my hand in both of hers. She told me how, with endless patience, a young falcon was taught to perch on the wrist, and how it gradually grew used to the leg straps with bells and the plumed hood.

“First they must have a good appetite,” she said. “Then, little by little, I reduce their nourishment, which in falconry we call feed. After many nights spent on a block perch, as these birds are now, I persuade the adult, wild-caught falcon to stay quietly on the wrist. Then it is ready to learn to come for its food. I fasten the feed to the end of a leather thong, or lure, and teach the bird to come to me as soon as I start whirling the cord in circles above my head. At first, when the falcon comes, I drop the feed, and it eats the food on the ground. Soon it will learn to seize the lure as I whirl it round my head or drag it along the ground. After that, teaching it to strike at game is easy. One must always remember to ‘give the bird its reward’, that is, let it taste the quarry.”
A squeal from one of the falcons interrupted her. She rose to adjust the leash, which had wound around the block perch, but the bird kept flapping its wings and screaming.
“What is the matter?” she asked. “Philip, can you see?”

I looked around. At first I saw nothing to explain the disturbance, which now grew louder as all the birds screamed and flapped. Then I noticed the flat rock beside the stream, where the girl had been sitting. A grey snake was moving slowly across it. The eyes in its flat, triangular head shone like jet.
“A snake,” she said quietly.
“It is harmless, isn’t it?” I asked.
She pointed to the black V-shaped mark on its neck.
“It is certain death,” she said. “It is a viper.”
We watched the reptile move slowly over the smooth rock towards a broad, warm patch of sunlight.
I started forward to examine it, but she clung to my arm, crying, “Don’t, Philip. I am afraid.”
“For me?”
“For you, Philip—I love you.”

Then I took her in my arms and kissed her lips, but all I could say was, “Jeanne, Jeanne, Jeanne.” As she lay trembling against my chest, something struck my foot in the grass below. I paid no attention. Then something struck my ankle again, and a sharp pain shot through me. I looked into Jeanne d’Ys’s sweet face and kissed her. With all my strength, I lifted her in my arms and flung her away from me. Then I bent, tore the viper from my ankle and put my heel on its head. I remember feeling weak and numb. I remember falling to the ground. Through my slowly glazing eyes, I saw Jeanne’s white face bending close to mine. When the light went out of my eyes, I still felt her arms around my neck and her soft cheek against my tightened lips.

When I opened my eyes, I looked around in terror. Jeanne was gone. I saw the stream and the flat rock. I saw the crushed viper in the grass beside me. But the hawks and their block perches had disappeared. I sprang to my feet. The garden, fruit trees, drawbridge and walled courtyard were gone. I stared stupidly at a heap of crumbling ruins, grey and covered in ivy, through which great trees had forced their way. I crept forward, dragging my numbed foot. As I moved, a falcon sailed from the treetops among the ruins. Soaring higher in narrowing circles, it faded and vanished into the clouds above.

“Jeanne, Jeanne,” I cried. But my voice died on my lips, and I fell to my knees among the weeds. As God willed it, I had unknowingly fallen kneeling before a crumbling stone shrine to our Mother of Sorrows. I saw the Virgin’s sad face carved in the cold stone. I saw the cross and thorns at her feet. Beneath it, I read:

“PRAY FOR THE SOUL OF THE
LADY JEANNE D’Ys,
WHO DIED
IN HER YOUTH FOR LOVE OF
PHILIP, A STRANGER.
IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1573.”
But on the icy slab lay a woman’s glove, still warm and fragrant.
